anchors.paper_title: An Open Dataset of Human Electroencephalographic and Behavioural Responses to Food Images
anchors.reason: Title nearly identical to the dataset's (FOODEEG), same authors and 117 participants; the bioRxiv preprint describes and releases this dataset.

metadata.methods_description: Session 1 recorded EEG (BDF format) while participants viewed food images for 2 s and made yes/no judgements of healthiness, tastiness, or willingness to eat. They then gave continuous 0-100 ratings of each image. Session 2 comprised a food go/no-go task, a food paired choice task, and questionnaires on dietary style, eating motivations, general motivational tendencies and hedonism. Normative ratings on 22 food attributes were collected separately from online samples (N = 624).

citation_details.title: The Centroparietal Positivity Traces the Path of Evidence Accumulation During Dietary Decisions
citation_details.author: Violet J Chae, Lauren Claire Fong, Tijl Grootswagers, Paul Michael Garrett, Stefan Bode, Daniel Feuerriegel
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Each day we make dozens of decisions about food. These choices are informed not only by information that we receive from our senses, but also by our memories, values, cultural norms, and goals. Evidence accumulation models have been proposed to explain how we transform these disparate sources of information into dietary choices and their corresponding motor actions. These models describe decisions arising from a noisy integration of decisional evidence until a criterion is reached. We investigated whether the centroparietal positivity (CPP), an event-related potential component proposed as a neural correlate of evidence accumulation during perceptual judgements, also traces accumulation trajectories during dietary decisions. citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
